questions.title: Memory Ownership practice 1
questions.prompt: What does `std::move` do to a unique_ptr?
choices: Transfers its ownership to the destination
Copies the owned object automatically
Deletes both pointers
Makes the object global
questions.explanation: Move transfers the unique ownership; the destination owns the object and the source becomes empty.

questions.title: Memory Ownership practice 2
choices: When several parts truly share ownership
For every local integer
Whenever a raw reference is enough
To avoid including memory
questions.explanation: A shared pointer models multiple owners whose lifetimes overlap, not ordinary temporary access to an object.

questions.title: Trace Memory Ownership
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: The unique pointer owns the Student, move transfers that ownership into active, and cleanup happens automatically when active leaves scope. The resulting output is 'Ada'.

questions.title: Memory Ownership practice 5
questions.prompt: What happens to the Student when `student` (a unique_ptr) goes out of scope?
choices: It is destroyed automatically, with no manual delete needed
It leaks unless you call delete student
It is copied, so two Students now exist
It stays alive until the program ends
questions.explanation: A `unique_ptr` owns its object and deletes it when the pointer leaves scope. That is the reason to prefer it over raw `new`: the cleanup is tied to the object's lifetime, so there is no `delete` to forget. A unique_ptr cannot be copied, and the object does not outlive its owner.

questions.title: Memory Ownership concept check 1
choices: `std::shared_ptr` uses a reference count and is appropriate when ownership is genuinely shared. Using it everywhere can hide unclear lifetime design and can leak cycles, so begin with values, containers, or unique ownership.
Use shared ownership when one clear owner exists.
Call `delete` manually for memory owned by a smart pointer.
Copy a unique owner as if two owners are allowed.
questions.explanation: `std::shared_ptr` uses a reference count and is appropriate when ownership is genuinely shared. Using it everywhere can hide unclear lifetime design and can leak cycles, so begin with values, containers, or unique ownership. This matters because ownership code depends on knowing which object owns memory and when that memory is released.

questions.title: Memory Ownership concept check 2
questions.prompt: Which choice describes a reliable Memory Ownership practice?
choices: Use raw new/delete for ordinary container data.
Prefer values and standard containers first.
Ignore move semantics when transferring ownership.
Store a pointer without deciding who owns the object.
questions.explanation: Prefer values and standard containers first. This matters because ownership code depends on knowing which object owns memory and when that memory is released.

questions.title: Memory Ownership concept check 3
questions.prompt: Which Memory Ownership code review note is accurate?
choices: Create a reference cycle with shared ownership.
Use a dangling pointer after the owner is gone.
Use make_unique for one dynamic owner.
Return a reference to a local object.
questions.explanation: Use make_unique for one dynamic owner. This matters because ownership code depends on knowing which object owns memory and when that memory is released.

questions.title: Memory Ownership concept check 4
questions.prompt: Which Memory Ownership habit prevents a common mistake?
choices: Choose dynamic allocation before trying stack values.
Share mutable ownership where borrowing would be clearer.
Hide ownership transfer inside a vague helper name.
Move unique ownership deliberately.
questions.explanation: Move unique ownership deliberately. This matters because ownership code depends on knowing which object owns memory and when that memory is released.

questions.title: Memory Ownership concept check 5
questions.prompt: Which Memory Ownership advice is accurate?
choices: Use shared ownership only when the model requires it.
Use `shared_ptr` to avoid designing lifetime.
Reset a smart pointer while other code still expects the object.
Mix raw and smart ownership for the same object.
questions.explanation: Use shared ownership only when the model requires it. This matters because ownership code depends on knowing which object owns memory and when that memory is released.

questions.title: Memory Ownership concept check 6
questions.prompt: Which statement is accurate about Memory Ownership?
choices: Forget that containers manage their own elements.
Use automatic lifetime and smart pointers to make resource responsibility clear.
Use manual cleanup when RAII would handle it.
Pass ownership when the function only needs to read.
questions.explanation: Use automatic lifetime and smart pointers to make resource responsibility clear. This matters because ownership code depends on knowing which object owns memory and when that memory is released.
